title: Shuffle an array
label: idb-list
statement: Build a shuffler for an array: `Shuffle()` returns a random ordering where **every possible ordering is equally likely**, and `Reset()` returns the original order.
provenance: **InterviewDB-listed.** LeetCode 384 is on the LinkedIn list you supplied from InterviewDB. No candidate report of this exact question was found in the research passes — the evidence is that the list names it. On that list it uses the same pattern as InterviewDB Q4, Q12. Fisher-Yates. Related to Q4 and Q12 through the same demand: every outcome equally likely, and a plausible-looking shortcut that is subtly biased. The classic wrong shuffle picks any index rather than one from the unshuffled tail.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Build a shuffler for an array: `Shuffle()` returns a random ordering where **every possible ordering is equally likely**, and `Reset()` returns the original order.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Must every permutation be exactly equally likely? (Yes.)
- May Shuffle return the same array object each time? (Return a copy.)
- Can I seed the random generator for tests? (Yes — take a Random.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Fisher–Yates: from the last position down, swap it with a random position **at or before it**. Each of the n! orderings comes out with probability exactly 1/n!. The common bug — swapping with any position 0..n−1 — produces nⁿ equally likely paths, and nⁿ is not divisible by n!, so some orders are favoured.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "F."isher–Yates: for i from the end, swap position i with a random j in 0..i; keep a private copy of the original for Reset — O(n) per shuffle, exactly uniform."

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Make the design decision yourself, then ask the assistant to attack it.
- Delegate the mechanical parts only after the structure is fixed.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe Fisher–Yates: for i from the end, swap position i with a random j in 0..i; keep a private copy of the original for Reset — O(n) per shuffle, exactly uniform. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Shuffle concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Swapping with `rnd.Next(n)` instead of `rnd.Next(i + 1)` — biased.
- Sorting by a random key — O(n log n), and biased if keys collide.
- Not copying the input, so Reset returns the caller's modified array.

learn.md:
**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Many threads shuffle.* — Each call must work on its own copy; System.Random is not thread-safe — use Random.Shared.
